facts.fact: Name for the term: "Đặc hữu"
Name for the term: "Endemism"
Endemism is the ecological condition in which an organism lives naturally only in one particular geographic location.

There are two kinds: palaeoendemics, species that once ranged more widely but now survive only in a smaller area, and neoendemics, new species that formed recently, for example through hybridisation (most often in plants).
Endemic species usually form through geographic isolation, for example on remote islands such as Hawaii, the Galápagos and Socotra.
In places rich in endemic species, the main threat is habitat loss from farming, urban growth, mining, logging and slash-and-burn farming.
Yale e360 describes how hobbyists keep fish endemic to small areas, such as the Lake Victoria basin, where about 200 fish species are thought to have disappeared.
The CARES Fish Preservation Program was launched in 2004 by North American hobbyists. It keeps a priority list of hundreds of at-risk species, compiled by regional or family experts.
CARES hobbyists register their fish in a central database, usually through regional aquarium clubs, and share husbandry information.
For CARES, breeding in captivity comes first and putting fish back into the wild is a secondary goal.
The finescale splitfin (Allodontichthys polylepis) was thought extinct in the wild by 2010, with eight fish in captivity. About 350 now exist, and a wild population was rediscovered in 2016.
The tequila splitfin (Zoogoneticus tequila) and the Potosi pupfish (Cyprinodon alvarezi), both kept by hobbyist programmes, have been put back into Mexican waters.
Small captive stocks can become genetically narrow (bottlenecks).
Over generations, fish in tanks can change into types suited to aquariums rather than the wild, with shifts in colour and feeding. Line breeding can speed this up.
Having captive populations can make people complacent about habitat loss, and collectors may take the last wild fish. Uganda banned exports after heavy collecting.
Keep a threatened species in more than one tank, so that losing one tank does not end the line.
Breed the fish and pass offspring to other keepers, since few people keep one line going for many years. Working with zoos and public aquariums also helps.
CARES stands for Conservation, Awareness, Recognition, Encouragement, and Support. It is made up of 30 national and international societies and organizations.
The CARES priority list includes 572 freshwater species. 30 of them are extinct in the wild, and over 80 are not yet scientifically described.
Cichlids make up nearly half of the CARES list, likely because they are popular and highly endemic to habitats under heavy human pressure.
Copadichromis sp. 'Firecrest Mloto' is believed extinct in the wild and survives only in the aquarium trade. The IUCN has not evaluated it because it is undescribed.
The Kisaki killifish (Nothobranchius flammicomantis) is on the CARES list and classed as Vulnerable by the IUCN.
Of the species the two groups rank differently, 7 that the IUCN rates 'least concern' are listed by CARES as extinct in the wild.
Many fish species that are extinct in the wild survive only because hobbyists keep and breed them.
About half of freshwater fish species have not been formally assessed, and freshwater fish are the most threatened group of vertebrates.
The Emerald Rainbowfish (Glossolepis wanamensis) is critically endangered and native to one lake in Papua New Guinea.
The Goodeid Working Group keeps 12 of the most endangered or extinct-in-the-wild goodeid species and 24 threatened ones in Mexico.

The Goodeid Working Group aims to keep existing goodeid populations and species in their natural forms. Members are expected to share breeding experience, and the group hopes surplus fish will stay available to members.

Protected species that need help should not be taken from the wild except under very specific, well-researched circumstances, because collecting can harm the remaining population and its genetic diversity.
Many native species need a cold winter period with short days, followed by gradual warming, which most home aquarists cannot reliably provide.
Keepers can help by breeding common native species, recording life-history details such as spawning temperature and egg size, sharing methods, and joining clubs such as NANFA.
Tanichthys sp. 'Vietnam' is known only from Da Nang province in central Vietnam. It was first collected in 2009 and may be undescribed.

Tanichthys sp. 'Vietnam' is sold as T. sp. 'lemon' or 'yellow white cloud' and has been confused with T. thacbaensis, a valid species from farther north in Vietnam. It has bright yellow ventral and anal fins. T. micagemmae has reddish ones, and T. albonubes has a reddish-brown body.
Tanichthys sp. 'Vietnam': 18–25°C, pH 6.0–7.5, 2–10 dGH. Keep a group of 10 or more in a tank with a base of at least 45 × 30 cm.
Tanichthys micagemmae is known only from the Ben Hai river system in north central Vietnam, mainly in Quang Tri province. The type specimens came from Quang Binh province.
Tanichthys micagemmae: 18–23 °C, pH 6.5–7.5, soft water at 2–8 dGH. It does well in a planted tank with dark substrate, floating plants, driftwood and leaf litter.
Tanichthys micagemmae is sold as 'Vietnamese minnow', 'cardinal minnow', 'royal white cloud' and 'dwarf cardinal'.
Annamia cf. thuathienensis was described from the Bô River in Thua Thien-Hue Province, central Vietnam, and no other records are listed.
Annamia cf. thuathienensis: 16–22°C, pH 6.0–7.5, 1–10 dGH. It needs high oxygen, strong flow, spotless water and weekly water changes of 30–50%.

Common mistakes with Annamia cf. thuathienensis: putting it in a biologically immature tank, buying emaciated fish, keeping fewer than about eight, and feeding only animal foods without Spirulina-based foods.

Wildlife At Risk (WAR), based in Ho Chi Minh City, reported 12 freshwater fish species new to Vietnam, found in Phu Quoc at the end of 2008. They include ca lia thia ap mieng (Betta prima) and pearl danio (Danio pulcher).
In early December 2010, WAR released over 100 Betta prima from its breeding programme into the Cau Do river, an estuary of the Sai Gon river.
